summary: Defines AgentX, a framework for extensible SNMP agents. It describes master agents and subagents, a protocol for them to communicate, and the procedures by which the combined agent handles SNMP messages. It was replaced by RFC 2741.

plainLanguage.summary: One main helper receives all the questions and hands each to a specialist helper who knows the answer, so many programs can share one network manager.

subtitle: A protocol for splitting SNMP agents into a master and specialized subagents.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to manage complex devices with many different types of instrumentation. Monolithic SNMP agents are difficult to extend and require all management code in a single process. Vendors want to develop agents independently without coordinating with each other.
tldr.mechanism: AgentX defines a master agent that communicates with SNMP managers, and a protocol by which independent subagents register MIB regions and handle management requests. The master agent forwards requests to the appropriate subagent based on the MIB tree structure.
tldr.outcome: Multiple independently developed subagents can coexist on a single host, each managing its own instrumentation. The master agent hides this complexity from SNMP managers. RFC 2257 was replaced by RFC 2741 with the same core concepts.

today: RFC 2257 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 2741, which carries forward AgentX version 1 with clarifications and refinements. AgentX remains the standard protocol for extensible SNMP agents.

sections.title: Extensible SNMP Agents
sections.content:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the standard for managing devices across networks. Traditional SNMP agents are monolithic: all the management instrumentation code runs in a single process. This makes it difficult to extend agents dynamically or to integrate management modules from different vendors.

The Agent Extensibility framework (AgentX) solves this by splitting an agent into two roles: a master agent that handles SNMP protocol messages and security, and one or more subagents that provide management information. Subagents are independent processes that can be installed, updated, or removed without restarting the master.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one giant database answering all questions, you have one receptionist (the master) who knows the SNMP rules, and many assistants (subagents) who each know about different things.

sections.title: Master Agents and Subagents
sections.content:
The master agent performs the SNMP role: it listens for incoming SNMP requests from managers on the network, enforces access control and security policies, and sends back responses. However, it does not directly provide most management information. Instead, it maintains a registry of which subagents handle which parts of the MIB (Management Information Base).

Each subagent registers one or more regions of the MIB tree with the master agent. When the master receives an SNMP request for a management object, it looks up the registered subagent for that region and sends an AgentX protocol message asking the subagent to provide or modify the requested object. The subagent processes the request using its own instrumentation and returns the result to the master, which then forms the SNMP response.

From a manager's perspective, the extensible agent behaves like a normal monolithic agent. The internal division of labor is invisible.
sections.plainLanguage: The master knows the rules of SNMP. Each subagent is an expert in one area, like disk management or network interfaces. When a question comes in, the master routes it to the right expert.

sections.title: Protocol and PDU Types
sections.content:
AgentX defines a binary protocol with Protocol Data Units (PDUs) for communication between master and subagent. Unlike SNMP, AgentX PDUs are not encoded using BER; they are compact, aligned binary structures optimized for local inter-process communication (though they can also run over TCP).

Key PDU types include: agentx-Open-PDU and agentx-Close-PDU for session management; agentx-Register-PDU for a subagent to claim MIB regions; agentx-Get-PDU, agentx-GetNext-PDU, and agentx-GetBulk-PDU for retrieval operations (mirroring SNMP operations); and agentx-TestSet-PDU, agentx-CommitSet-PDU, and related PDUs for modification operations. Each session between a master and subagent is identified by a unique session ID, and each SNMP request is tracked by a transaction ID so responses can be matched to requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The master and subagents speak a special language of messages to coordinate. One message type says 'connect', another says 'I handle this part of the tree', another says 'get this object', and so on.

sections.title: Request Dispatching and Procedures
sections.content:
When the master agent receives an SNMP GetRequest for an object, it searches its registry to find which subagent (if any) has registered that MIB region. A deterministic dispatching algorithm ensures that exactly one subagent is authoritative for any region. The master sends an agentx-Get-PDU to that subagent, which retrieves the value and returns an agentx-Response-PDU. The master then assembles the SNMP response and sends it to the manager.

For SNMP SetRequest operations (modifications), AgentX uses a two-phase commit protocol: the master first sends an agentx-TestSet-PDU to the subagent to check if the proposed change is valid, then (if all subagents approve) sends an agentx-CommitSet-PDU to apply the change. If any subagent rejects the test, the master can send agentx-UndoSet-PDU to roll back any partial changes.

This architecture supports typical deployment scenarios: subagents implementing separate MIB modules, subagents sharing table rows, and subagents registering different parts of a large MIB tree.
sections.plainLanguage: When a manager asks 'what is the CPU load', the master finds which subagent knows about CPU, asks it, gets the answer, and sends it back. If the manager wants to change something, the master asks all affected subagents 'okay to change', and only makes the change if they all say yes.

sections.title: Security Model
sections.content:
AgentX does not define authentication between master and subagent; it delegates that to the transport layer. If the master and subagent run on the same host using local transport (Unix domain sockets, named pipes, or shared memory), operating system access controls determine which processes can connect. If a network transport is used, the RFC recommends using TLS or other mechanisms (outside the scope of AgentX itself).

AgentX also does not define access control for which subagents can register which MIB regions. The RFC notes this as a potential security concern: a malicious subagent could register a sensitive subtree and eavesdrop on modification attempts or return false information. For this reason, the RFC recommends running subagents only on the same host as the master agent, where operating system privilege boundaries can enforce authorization.

The master agent retains full responsibility for SNMP security policies (authentication, access control, and view-based authorization) and does not share security credentials with subagents.
sections.plainLanguage: AgentX trusts that the subagents are allowed to be there; it does not verify credentials itself. So you need to make sure only trusted programs can connect as subagents, using your operating system's permissions.
